identity.name: Calcium phosphates
identity.chemical_class: Inorganic calcium salts of phosphoric acid

function.mechanism: Dissociates in aqueous solution to release calcium and phosphate ions. Monocalcium phosphate is acidic (acid component in baking powder). Tricalcium phosphate is mildly basic and acts as anti-caking agent. All forms provide calcium and phosphorus fortification.
common_food_categories: Powdered food mixes and dry seasonings

adi.basis: Group ADI expressed as phosphorus. Derived from NOAEL of 167 mg P/kg bw/day (chronic rat nephrocalcinosis study) with chemical-specific adjustment factor of 4 and phosphorus-specific uncertainty factor of 4. Applies to total phosphorus from all dietary sources.

efsa.key_finding: Low acute oral toxicity, no genotoxicity or carcinogenicity concern, no reproductive/developmental toxicity. Critical adverse effect is renal calcification and tubular nephropathy. ADI exceeded in infants, toddlers, and children at mean exposure. ADI not applicable to individuals with moderate-to-severe reduced renal function (~10% of population).

fda.notes: Calcium phosphate (mono-, di-, and tribasic) is GRAS when used in accordance with good manufacturing practice. No quantitative limits specified.

adi.basis: Maximum Tolerable Daily Intake (MTDI, not ADI) expressed as phosphorus for the sum of all phosphates naturally present in food and used as additives. Applicable to diets nutritionally adequate in calcium.

concerns.summary: Nephrocalcinosis and tubular nephropathy in chronic rat studies. In humans, doses of 4,800 mg P/day (68.6 mg/kg/day) caused renal impairment. High acute single doses (≥160 mg P/kg bw) can induce renal impairment. The EFSA ADI is explicitly not protective for individuals with impaired renal function.
key_references: Hodge (1960) — chronic rat study, NOAEL 76 mg P/kg bw/day

concerns.summary: Elevated serum phosphate associated with cardiovascular risk markers (FGF23, PTH elevation, vascular calcification, left ventricular hypertrophy) in both CKD patients and general population. Inorganic phosphate from additives has 80-90% bioavailability vs 40-60% from natural sources, disproportionately raising serum levels. Epidemiological associations exist but causation not established.
key_references: Cupisti A et al. (2025) Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 20(9):1289-1298

no_concern_confirmed: Genotoxicity — comprehensive in vitro and in vivo test battery showed no concern (EFSA 2019)
Carcinogenicity — no carcinogenic potential in long-term animal studies (EFSA 2019)
Reproductive and developmental toxicity — no effects at any dose tested in mice, rats, rabbits, hamsters (EFSA 2019)

populations: Infants (12 weeks to 11 months) — exceeded at mean exposure
People with chronic kidney disease (~10% of population) — ADI not applicable
adi_exceedance.notes: The EFSA 2019 ADI of 40 mg P/kg bw/day encompasses total phosphorus from all dietary sources (natural + additive). Because phosphorus is ubiquitous in the diet, the ADI is commonly exceeded in young populations even without heavy additive use. The German SKLM (2026) confirmed these concerns and recommended risk management measures for vulnerable groups.

risk_assessment.rationale: Calcium phosphates are universally approved, essential nutrients (calcium + phosphorus), with no genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, or reproductive toxicity. GRAS in the US with no quantitative limits. Not classified by IARC. No bans anywhere. However, EFSA established a specific group ADI (40 mg P/kg bw/day) in 2019 that is exceeded in children and adolescents. The ADI is explicitly not protective for ~10% of the population with impaired renal function. Emerging evidence links high inorganic phosphate intake to cardiovascular risk markers. These factors prevent a 'risk_free' classification but the overall safety profile is strong, warranting 'limited' rather than 'moderate'.
key_factors: Essential nutrients — provides calcium and phosphorus
GRAS status in US, approved in EU, no bans worldwide
No genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, or reproductive toxicity
EFSA group ADI of 40 mg P/kg bw/day exceeded in young populations
Renal effects (nephrocalcinosis) are the critical endpoint
ADI not protective for CKD patients (~10% of population)
Inorganic phosphate from additives has higher bioavailability than natural sources
